## Results

The hydrothermal conversion of NaHCO3 into organics was conducted in a stainless steel autoclave with an inner volume of 7 mL at 250°C for 12 h, with 1 MPa H2 serving as the reducing agent. The resulting products were identified through GC−MS and NMR analyses following acidification or derivatization (Supplementary Fig. 3−63). Drawing inspiration from the transition metal-sulfur coordination structure of CO2-immobilized enzymes, we screened various sulfide minerals for their potential role in the prebiotic CO2 RN. Among the tested minerals (FeS2, Ni3S2, Cu2S, CuS, CoS, CoS2, MnS, 2H-MoS2, and 1Tʹ-MoS2), the twisted 1Tʹ-MoS2 polymorph, which mimics the distorted geometry of the carbon dioxide Mo-S-pterin enzyme23 and Mo-nitrogenase24 that produce hydrocarbons under certain conditions (Supplementary Fig. 64), enables the hydrothermal conversion of NaHCO3 into formate, acetate, glycolate, oxalate, propionate, lactate, 2-hydroxybutanoate, succinate, and methylsuccinate (Supplementary Figs. 3−61). Given the instability of pyruvate and other reaction products, the reaction temperature was reduced or the reaction time was shortened to identify additional intermediates. When the reaction time was shortened to 3 h, several additional compounds, including α-ketoglutarate, 3-hydroxybutanoate, crotonate, butyrate, fumarate, methylmalonate, 4-hydroxybutyrate, 3-hydroxypropionate, and hydroxyisobutyrate, were detected (Supplementary Fig. 65−96). At lower temperatures of 70°C and 100°C, further products such as pyruvate, acetoacetate, acetaldehyde, glyoxylate, methacrylate, ehtylmalonate, mesaconate, malonate, malate, itaconate and isobutyrate were identified (Supplementary Fig. 97−161).

Using intermediates and end-products of the ancient acetyl-CoA pathway (formate, acetate, and pyruvate) as substrates, all the aforementioned products of hydrothermal NaHCO3 reduction were reproduced, along with additional compounds β-methylmalate and citraconate at 70°C over 12 h during pyruvate conversion (Supplementary Figs. 162−207). This supports the central role of acetyl-CoA in protometabolic carbon fixation. A total of 32 products were synthesized from NaHCO3, encompassing 7 out of 11 products from the rTCA cycle, 9 out of 13 products from the 3HP-4HB pathway, 9 out of 11 products from the DC-4HB pathway, 6 out of the 9 intermediates of the glyoxylate cycle and all intermediates of the EMCP. The isotopic labeling studies using NaH13CO3, combined with GC–MS analysis validated by authentic standards and spiking experiments, confirmed that all intermediates originated from a single carbon source (Supplementary Fig. 208−244). Based on the product analysis, a fundamental chemical autocatalytic network for carbon fixation was constructed (Fig. 1), enabling a one-step conversion from CO2/NaHCO3 to multi-carbon carboxylic acids, specifically all five universal metabolic precursors (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1). This observation of direct nonenzymatic CO2 conversion surpasses previous attempts to construct rTCA chemical reaction networks, which required both active pyruvate and glyoxylate as substrates16.

The variation of Gibbs free energy (ΔG) of the reactions under saturated vapor pressure at different temperatures was calculated based on the existing database (Supplementary Fig. 245; For detailed datasets, see Supplementary Table 2). Most reactions are thermodynamically favorable (ΔG < 0) under specific temperature conditions. For reactions generating malate, fumarate, succinate, α-ketoglutarate, oxalate, methylmalonate, and hydroxyisobutyrate (ΔG > 0), higher pressure from hydrogen replenishment and the consumption of these organics within reaction networks drive these reactions away from equilibrium.

To gain a deeper understanding of the transforming relationship in the prebiotic CO2 RN, we evaluated the effects of various parameters—including reaction temperature, time, NaHCO3 concentration, hydrogen pressure, and catalyst amount—on the production of formic acid in the acetyl-CoA pathway and five universal intermediates and their derivatives involved in C−C coupling (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 246). When the temperature is below 200°C, the primary products are C1−C3 compounds such as formate, acetate, propionate, and lactate (Fig. 2a). When the temperature exceeds 200°C, succinate and methylsuccinate begin to appear, indicating that higher temperatures promote the C−C coupling process. Pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate are detected only at lower temperatures, which aligns with existing literature9. Higher temperatures lead to the reduction of pyruvate to lactate, a phenomenon not observed in previous studies of prebiotic CO2 fixation6,9,26.

The acetate, which links acetyl-CoA, rTCA, 3HP-4HB, and DC-4HB, was primarily generated from formate (Fig. 2b, bottom panel), indicating that the acetyl-CoA pathway was the initial reaction to occur, consistent with the autocatalytic network described above. Another universal metabolic precursor, α-ketoglutarate, regenerated when the reaction time was extended to 24 h at 250°C, suggesting the presence of a dynamic reaction network (Supplementary Figs. 247−253). The selectivity of C2+ carboxylic acids in the time-dependent experiment exhibited an oscillatory distribution (Fig. 2b, upper panel), reflecting the characteristics of natural autocatalytic networks involved in carbon cycling27. The observation of oscillatory behavior not only enhances the diversity of reaction pathways but also increases the overall complexity of the reactions. Such properties may have significant implications for carbon cycling during the origin and evolution of early life, as they expand the array of possible chemical interactions and pathways that could have contributed to life’s emergence28.

The excessive use of substrates NaHCO3 (Fig. 2c) or H2 (Fig. 2d) decreased the selectivity for C2+ products, consistent with previous findings that high hydrogen pressure inhibited C−C coupling29, leading to formate as the dominant product. This observation indicated that formate/formyl was not responsible for C−C coupling, which differed from the previous study involving the formyl radical mechanism21. Additionally, optimizing the amount of catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 254) led to a CO2 conversion rate of 68.6% and a selectivity of 74.5% for C2+ products (Fig. 2e), which exceeded the performance of catalysts previously reported for CO2/NaHCO3 conversion (Supplementary Table 3). Notably, the catalyst demonstrated catalytic turnover over 21 consecutive cycles, with a cumulative turnover number (TON) of 1.02. When adjusted for the proportion of active Mo3+ sites (~58%), the effective TON reached 1.76, unequivocally confirming true catalytic behavior (Supplementary Fig. 255).

To elucidate the origin of the outstanding performance of CO2 RN, the atomic and electronic structure of 1Tʹ-MoS2 was investigated. The 1Tʹ-MoS2 was synthesized hydrothermally, as the geological conditions, such as high temperature and pressure or strong stress, can induce the structural transformation from 2H to 1T phase30. The XRD analysis revealed a peak corresponding to the typical 002 plane of the 1T phase, with a d-spacing of 9.4Å (Supplementary Fig. 256, Supplementary Table 4)31. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) analysis confirmed the interlayer spacing and lattice fringes, showing structures with d-spacings of 0.64 nm (attributed to 2H phase) and 0.94 nm (attributed to 1T phase) in the 1T′-MoS2 sample (Supplementary Fig. 257)32. The enlarged HRTEM image clearly displayed the triangular atomic arrangement of the 1T phase, corroborating the XRD analysis33. The 1T phase in 1Tʹ-MoS2 was also confirmed by photoluminescence (PL), ultraviolet–visible (UV−Vis), and Raman spectroscopy. The PL spectra showed the absence of peaks attributed to interlayer coupling and spin-orbit coupling of the 2H phase in 1T′-MoS2 (Supplementary Fig. 258)34. The UV−vis spectrum of 1T′-MoS2 exhibited a monotonic change without absorption peaks at 635 nm, 458 nm, and 400 nm, which are characteristic of the 2H phase (Supplementary Fig. 259). The Raman peaks at 200 (J1), 225 (J2), 336 (J3), and 355 (J3) cm−1 were consistent with the formation of 1T phase containing Mo3+ (Fig. 3a)35.

The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis showed that the binding energy of the Mo 3d peaks in 1Tʹ-MoS2 was ∼1 eV lower than that in 2H-MoS2, indicating the formation of Mo3+ (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 260). Further deconvolution of the XPS Mo 3d spectra revealed that the 1T phase content was 58.0% ± 0.5% in 1Tʹ-MoS2, confirming Mo3+ as the predominant species (Supplementary Table 5)35. The formation of Mo3+ was also corroborated by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) analysis. The EPR spectra of 1Tʹ-MoS2 showed a signal centered at g=2.014, typical of Mo3+36, distinct from sulfide-related paramagnetic states (g=2.002) of 2H phase (Fig. 3c)37. The Mo K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra showed that the absorption edge energy (defined as the energy where the normalized absorption is 0.5) for the 1Tʹ-MoS2 was lower than that of the 2H phase, supporting the presence of Mo3+ (Fig. 3d). The fitting of X-ray absorption fine structure data revealed the decreased coordination number of Mo−S in 1Tʹ-MoS2 compared to that of 2H-MoS2, suggesting the existence of sulfur vacancy (Supplementary Figs. 261−263, Supplementary Table 6). The presence of the sulfur vacancies in 1Tʹ-MoS2 was further confirmed by aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (AC-TEM) (Fig. 3e), where some sulfur atoms octahedrally coordinated to Mo were not observed (light green dashed circle). The electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) (Fig. 3f) showed that the electron energy loss of Mo-M5, Mo-M4, Mo-M3, Mo-M2, and S-L2,3 edge in layer 1Tʹ region (Area 2) shown in Fig. 3f, located at 228, 234, 396, 414, and 164 eV, respectively, were lower than those in the 2H region (Area 1), further confirming the formation of Mo3+ in 1Tʹ-MoS238.

Compared to that of 1T’-MoS2, 2H-MoS2 primarily catalyzed NaHCO3 to organics dominated by formate, and the selectivity of C2+ products decreased by 8.1-fold (Fig. 4a). To elucidate the mechanism behind phase-induced CO2 RN, diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) was employed to detect key reaction intermediates (Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Figs. 264−265). The C–H stretching region (3200–2850 cm−1) in FTIR spectra showed distinct characteristics between 1T′- and 2H-MoS2 (Fig. 4b). The 1T phase displayed a methane-derived C–H vibrational mode, νasym(CH3), νsym(CH3), νasym(CH2), and νsym(CH2) stretching modes at 3016, 2958, 2927, and 2862 cm−1, respectively, as a function of reaction temperature and time39,40. These observations suggest the preferential stabilization of CHx intermediates, facilitating the formation of long-chain organics41. In contrast, no peaks corresponding to adsorbed CHx species were detected in 2H-MoS2, which aligns with the low selectivity of C2+ products.

The carbon monoxide (CO), proposed as the precursor of CHx in hydrogenation, was observed in the FTIR spectra of both 1T′- and 2H-MoS2. The peaks located at 2171 and 2115 cm−1 were assigned to CO vibrations42, while the peak at 2188 cm−1 was associated with surface-bound CO coordinated to Mo sites (Fig. 4b)43. Quantitative analysis by deconvolution (Fig. 4c) revealed a higher content of surface-bound CO (69.74%) in the 1T′ phase compared to that of 2H-MoS2 (44.51%). The enhanced CO adsorption on 1T′-MoS2 can be attributed to the dynamic involvement of hydroxyl groups, as demonstrated by the time-dependent modulation of the terminal Mo–OH vibration at 3730 cm−1 (octahedral coordination) and the Mo–OH bending mode at 900 cm−144,45. Surface hydroxyl groups are believed to interact with carbonaceous species to enhance their adsorption affinity46. The CO2 and CO temperature-programmed desorption measurements confirmed that the 1T′-MoS2 facilitates the adsorption of carbonaceous species (Supplementary Figs. 266–267). Operando spectral analysis also revealed the simultaneous consumption and regeneration of bicarbonate-associated hydroxyl groups (3703−3600 cm−1) and the catalytically active Mo–OH species43, thereby supporting a self-sustaining catalytic cycle47. The increased concentration of surface-bound CO promotes the formation of CHx intermediates and subsequent C–C coupling reactions. In contrast, the absence of hydroxyl groups in 2H-MoS2 reduces the adsorption strength of carbonaceous species, resulting in the formation of formate via the reaction of free CO with hydroxide ions (CO + OH− → HCOO−). These findings are consistent with the phase-dependent performance illustrated in Fig. 4a.

EPR spectroscopy was performed to identify the forms of species observed in FTIR. Upon heating the solution, the formation of formyl radical (CH•), acetyl radical (CH3CO•), propionyl radical (CH3CH2CO•), and hydroxyl radical (OH•) was first observed at 150°C, and further increased as the reaction temperature was raised to 250°C in 1T′-MoS2-catalyzed CO2 RN (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Figs. 268−269). Without adding the NaHCO3 substrate, no EPR signals were detected, confirming that the radicals originated from NaHCO3 reduction (Supplementary Fig. 270). When the phenyl-tert-butylnitrone (PBN) radical scavenger (1 time the amount of NaHCO3) was added into the 1T′ MoS2-catalyzed CO2 RN system, the yield of organics decreased by 3.7-fold, and further increasing the concentration of PBN (4 times the amount of NaHCO3) led to complete suppressing of C–C coupling (Fig. 4e). Additionally, the reduced activity of radical formation (Fig. 4d) catalyzed by 2H-MoS2 correlated with the poor performance of CO2 RN. These observations suggested that the radicals served as active intermediates and radical-mediated C–C coupling mechanisms were involved in 1T′-MoS2-catalyzed CO2 RN system. Collectively, the 1T′-MoS2 with vacancy-induced distorted octahedral structure promotes the formation of radicals from adsorbed CO reduction and enhances their adsorption and coupling in aqueous solutions.

The first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to further elucidate the underlying mechanism difference of phase-dependent CO2 RN. CH3 and CO are commonly chosen as monomer species in C–C coupling reactions, and both were detected in our experimental studies. We first examined the adsorption energies of CH3 and CO on sulfur-deficient 1T′-MoS2 and pristine 2H-MoS2 (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 271). The results show that CH3 has a lower adsorption energy than CO on all MoS2 structures, suggesting a stronger affinity for CH3 to interact with MoS2. The introduction of sulfur defects decreases the adsorption energies of both CH3 and CO on MoS2, with the adsorption energy of CH3 reaching −4.44 eV on 1T′-MoS2 and −2.63 eV on 2H-MoS2, respectively. Experimental observations also demonstrated that increasing the sulfur vacancy concentration in 1T′-MoS2 enhances the selectivity for C2+ products (Supplementary Figs. 272−273). Specifically, as the S:Mo ratio decreases from 1.85 to 1.79, the selectivity for C2+ products increases from 67.59% to 74.77% (Supplementary Table 5). These findings suggest that the Mo sites in MoS2 serve as the primary active sites for the activation of carbon-containing species.

To investigate the impact of sulfur vacancies on product selectivity, we calculated the activation energy for CH3−CO coupling on both pristine MoS2 and 1T′-MoS2 with sulfur vacancies. Specifically, we examined the influence of different catalytic reaction mechanisms, the Langmuir–Hinshelwood (L−H) and Eley–Rideal (E−R) mechanisms, where the L−H mechanism represents high sulfur vacancy density, while the E−R mechanism represents low sulfur vacancy density in MoS2 (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 274). Fig. 5b shows that the presence of sulfur vacancies significantly enhances the activity for C−C coupling, both thermodynamically and kinetically, as evidenced by the reduction in both adsorption energy and activation energy. Compared to 2H-MoS2, we found that 1T′-MoS2 exhibits superior reactivity, with the lowest activation energy of 1.18 eV during C−C coupling via the L−H mechanism. Regarding the adsorption configuration, the C−C distance between the CH3 and CO monomers is 2.56 Å on 1T′-MoS2 and 3.12 Å on 2H-MoS2, which aligns with previous theoretical studies that a shorter C−C distance is expected to lower the activation energy for C−C coupling48.

We next analyzed the electronic structures of both sulfur-deficient 1T′-MoS2 and 2H-MoS2 to elucidate the origins of their catalytic activity for C−C coupling reactions. Fig. 5c presents a comparison of the partial density of states (PDOS) between 1T′- and 2H-MoS2. The Mo d-orbitals in 1T′-MoS2 display a more discrete structure than that in 2H-MoS2, with the d-band center shifting from −0.88 eV in 2H-MoS2 to −0.69 eV in 1T′-MoS2. The shift with the d-band center approaching the Fermi level in 1T′-MoS2 suggests an enhancement in catalytic activity. Moreover, the work function of 1T′-MoS2 is lower (4.65 eV) compared to that of 2H-MoS2 (5.41 eV), indicating that electrons at the Mo sites in 1T′-MoS2 are more readily transferred to carbon-based species, thereby facilitating their activation (Supplementary Fig. 275). Additionally, the orbital interactions between the CH3 group and the Mo site were examined, as the Mo site exhibited the lowest adsorption energy for CH3 (Fig. 5a). In 1T′-MoS2, there exists a greater overlap between the Mo d-orbitals and the CH3 p-orbitals below the Fermi level compared to that of 2H-MoS2, suggesting stronger d−p hybridization (Fig. 5d). This phenomenon is further corroborated by crystal orbital Hamiltonian populations (COHP) analysis (Fig. 5e), which reveals a more negative integrated COHP value for the Mo−C bond in 1T′-MoS2 (−2.06 eV) relative to 2H-MoS2 (−0.66 eV), implying stronger Mo−CH3 interactions in 1T′-MoS2. Charge density and electron localization function (ELF) (Fig. 5f−g) analyses also show significant differences between 1T′ and 2H-MoS2. Notably, the regions near the Mo sites in 1T′-MoS2 exhibit a lower charge density and smaller ELF values, indicating more delocalized electron distributions, which may facilitate charge carrier transfer. Moreover, Bader charge analysis (Fig. 5h) supports these findings, showing that CH3 accepts 0.43 |e| from 1T′-MoS2, whereas only 0.21 |e| is transferred from 2H-MoS2. In addition, CO accepts 0.32 |e| from 1T′-MoS2, in contrast to only 0.15 |e| transferred from 2H-MoS2. Based on integrated experimental and spectroscopic analyses of catalytically active intermediates, we propose a visual summary (Fig. 5i) illustrating the key steps in the C−C bond formation between CH3 and CO on the 1T-MoS2 catalyst surface.

## Methods

Chemicals

L-cysteine (C3H7NO2S, ≥99.0%), nickel disulfide (NiS2, ≥99.0%), cobalt disulfide (CoS2, ≥99.5%), cobalt sulfide (CoS, ≥99.5%), 1,1,1,3,3,3-hexamethyldisilazane (C6H19NSi2, ≥99.0%), manganese sulfide (MnS, ≥99.5%), chlorotrimethylsilane (C3H9ClSi, ≥99.0%), crotonate (C4H6O2, ≥99.0%), hydroxyisobutyrate (C4H8O3, ≥98.0%), ethylmalonate (C5H8O4, ≥98.0%), and pyridine (C5H5N, ≥99.5%) were purchased from Beijing Enocai Technology Co., LTD. Ethanol (C2H5OH, ≥99.8%), methanol (CH3OH, ≥99.5%), propionate (C3H6O2, ≥99.5%), oxalate (C2H2O4, 1 mol/L), lactate (C3H6O3, 1 mol/L), succinate (C4H6O4, ≥99.5%), sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3, ≥99%), sodium bicarbonate-13C (NaH13CO3, ≥99.0%), and sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 95.0–98.0%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Sodium pyruvate-13C (13C3H3O3Na, ≥99.0%) were purchased from J&K scientific Technology Co., LTD. Formate (CH2O2, ≥98.0%), acetate (C2H4O2, ≥99.5%), glycolate (C2H4O3, ≥98.0%), fumarate (C4H4O4, ≥99.0%), glyoxylate (C2H2O3, 50% in water) were purchased Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. Methylsuccinate (C5H8O4, ≥99.5%), α-Ketoglutarate (C5H5NaO5, ≥99.5%), butyrate (C4H8O2, ≥99.0%), isobutyrate (C4H8O2, ≥99.0%), acetaldehyde (C2H4O, 40% in water) were purchased Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Hydrogen (H2, 99.999%), nitrogen (N2, 99.999%), and helium (He, 99.999%) were purchased from Shanghai Weichuang Standard Gas Analysis Technology Co., LTD.

Synthesis of metallic 1T′-MoS2
1T′-MoS2 in this work was synthesized using a hydrothermal method similar to previously described procedures37,49. In brief, 6 mmol of sodium molybdate and 6 mmol of L-cysteine were dissolved in 60 mL of ultrapure water (18.25 MΩ, Sichuan UPU Ultrapure Technology Co. Ltd). The mixture was stirred magnetically for 10 min and then transferred to a Teflon-lined 100 mL stainless steel autoclave reactor (Anhui Kemi Instrument Co., Ltd). The hydrothermal treatment was conducted at 200°C for 20 h, after which the reactor was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The resulting black precipitates were collected by filtration, thoroughly washed three times with ultrapure water and ethanol, and then lyophilized. Finally, the black solid was freeze-dried for 12 h.

NaHCO3 fixation catalyzed by 1T′-MoS2
The hydrothermal conversion of NaHCO3 to carboxylic acids was carried out in a stainless steel (SUS-316) autoclave with a 7 mL inner volume. The parameters such as temperature, reaction time, substrate concentration, water volume, and hydrogen pressure were varied according to the experimental design. The reactor was magnetically stirred at a speed of 800 rpm. After the reaction was completed, the gas, liquid, and solid products were cooled to room temperature by air cooling and then collected from the reactor. To verify the reaction pathways, NaH13CO3 and 13C3H3O3Na were also applied to the secondary experiments following the above steps. For comparison, 2H-MoS2 was used for the experiments following the above steps.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis
The liquid products were obtained by filtering through a 0.22-μm membrane filter and then were quantified on an Agilent 1200 system high−performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) equipped with two KC-811 columns (SHODEX) and a tunable UV−vis absorbance detector, which was set at 210 nm. A 2 mmol/L HClO4 solution was applied as the mobile phase at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min at 75°C. The HPLC external standard method was employed for quantitative analysis, which involved the preparation of a series of standard solutions with known concentrations of the analyte, followed by HPLC analysis to establish a calibration curve relating peak responses to concentrations. Subsequently, the same chromatographic conditions were applied to analyze the samples, and the concentration of the target analyte in the samples was determined by referencing the calibration curve.

Gas chromatography−mass spectrometry (GC−MS) analysis
After the reaction, the resulting liquid was adjusted to an acidic state (pH ~3) using H2SO4 and then esterified with either ethanol or methanol. The prepared sample was analyzed using an Agilent 7890A GC equipped with an Agilent 19091N-233 HP-Innowax Polyethylene Glycol column (30 m × 250 μm × 0.5 μm) and a model 5975C mass selective detector. The analysis was carried out in a splitless mode with a 1 μL injection volume, at an injection port temperature of 250°C. The column was maintained at 60°C for 1 min, then ramped up to 230°C at a rate of 7°C per minute, and was held at this final temperature for 40 min. Helium was used as the carrier gas. Formate, acetate, lactate, propionate, succinate, methyl succinate, glycolate, and oxalate were detected. To identify more compounds, some of the liquid products were acidified with HCl (pH ~3), frozen using liquid nitrogen, and further freeze-dried and concentrated. The esterified samples were then subjected to GC−MS analysis using the method described above. Lactate, pyruvate, butyrate, isobutyrate, fumarate, methylmalonate, crotonate, glyoxylate, acetaldehyde, malonate, methacrylate, 3-hydroxybutyrate, α-ketoglutarate, hydroxyisobutyrate, itaconate, methylmalate, and malate were detected. Additionally, some liquid products were silanized according to methods described in the literature and analyzed using GC−MS equipped with an Agilent 19091S-433 HP-5MSI Polyethylene Glycol column (30 m × 250 μm × 0.25 μm)50. The GC temperature program started at 35°C for 5 min, ramped to 320°C at 5°C min−1, and was held at this temperature for 10 min. Oxalate, malonate, itaconate, hydroxyisobutyrate, citraconate, lactate, glycolate, succinate, methyl succinate, ethylmalonate, mesaconate, α-ketoglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionate, and 4-hydroxybutyrate were detected. The corresponding isotope-labeled products were also qualitatively analyzed by GC−MS. The obtained mass spectra of the liquid products were analyzed using GC–MS post-run analysis software with commercial MS libraries. To reach the detection limit of GC−MS, we conducted sample freeze-drying and concentration, followed by derivatization for detection (a physical volume concentration factor of 3). These samples include: fumarate, methylmalonate, crotonate, glyoxylate, acetaldehyde, malonate, methacrylate, 3-hydroxybutyrate, hydroxyisobutyrate, itaconate, methylmalate, malate, itaconate, hydroxyisobutyrate, citraconate, ethylmalonate, mesaconate, α-ketoglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionate, and 4-hydroxybutyrate.

NMR analysis
1H NMR spectra were recorded at ambient temperature using a Bruker AVANCE III (600 MHz) spectrometer, employing a mixture (H2O/D2O: 6/1) as the solvent. The proton resonance frequency was 600.13 MHz. The main magnetic field was 14.09 Tesla (superconducting). The swept field range ranged from −1 to 13 ppm for 1H. Data were basically acquired 32 times with a recycle time of 7.6 s for a particle sample. A Diff50 RF double resonance diffusion probe was used with a gradient field strength of 28 T/m. Propionate and lactate were identified by adding an internal standard. Formate, acetate, succinate, methyl succinate, and ethanol were determined according to the literature51,52. Additionally, 13C-NMR data were obtained to determine the source of carbon according to the literatur53. The swept field range ranged from −12 to 220 ppm for 13C. Data were basically acquired 16 times. The rest of the conditions are the same as above.

Calculation of the product yield and selectivity
Product conversion was defined on the carbon-atom basis of NaHCO3:
Product yield = (nC in COOH / nNaHCO3) × 100% (1)
C2+ products selectivity was calculated based on the proportion of C2+ products among C2+ carboxylates:
C2+ selectivity = (Σ nC in COOH / Σ nC in COOH) × 100% (2)

X-ray diffraction analysis
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded using a Shimadzu XRD-6100PC, equipped with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.54184 Å) operating at 40 kV and 40 mA. The scanning angle (2θ) was set from 10° to 80°, with a scan rate of 2° per minute and step intervals of 0.01°.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
XPS spectra were obtained on an ESCALAB 250xi spectrometer equipped with a non-monochromatic Al Kα (photon energy 1486.6 eV) anode target. Conditions: vacuum, 1×10−8 bar; scanning range of binding energy, 0−1000 eV; pass energy, 40 eV; scanning step size, 0.1 eV/step.

Electron microscope measurements
HRTEM images were obtained using a JEOL JEM-2100F electron microscope at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The TEM samples were prepared by dropping the sample suspension onto a lacey carbon TEM grid, followed by air drying. HAADF-STEM (High-Angle Annular Dark-Field Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy) and EDS elemental mapping were conducted using an X-max Oxford electron microscope at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV.

Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope (AC-TEM)
The structural and chemical characterization was performed using a spherical aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) operated at 200 kV. The microscope is equipped with an integrated differential phase contrast (iDPC-STEM) imaging system, which employs a four-segment detector to record electron beam deflection signals generated by the sample’s electrostatic potential gradients. The iDPC-STEM configuration enables atomic-resolution imaging with low electron dose (≤10 e/Å2), critical for minimizing beam-sensitive damage in materials such as MOFs and 2D layered compounds. For elemental and chemical state analysis, electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) was conducted in STEM mode using a dual-EELS acquisition system with an energy resolution of 0.7 eV. The EELS spectra were collected over an energy range of 0−2000 eV, covering core-loss edges for light (e.g., C-K at 284 eV, O-K at 532 eV) and heavy elements. To enhance signal-to-noise ratio, multiple spectra (≥50 frames) were acquired with a dwell time of 0.1−0.5 ms/pixel and processed via background subtraction using power-law fitting. The EELS spatial mapping was synchronized with high-angle annular dark-field imaging to correlate atomic-scale structure with localized chemical information.

XAFS tests
XAFS data for the sample, as well as the metal and oxide references, were collected in raw transmission mode at Super Photon Ring-8 (SPring-8) in Japan. Pellet samples for the XAFS measurements were prepared by mixing granular samples with boron nitride (BN) from Kojundo Chemical Lab, Japan. The XANES spectra were derived by subtracting the post-edge background from the overall absorption signal and then normalizing the results with respect to the edge-jump step. The χ(k) data were subsequently Fourier transformed to real (R) space using Hanning windows (dk=1.0 Å−1) to isolate the EXAFS contributions from different coordination shells. To obtain quantitative structural parameters around the central atoms, least-squares curve fitting was performed using the ARTEMIS module of the IFEFFIT software package54,55.

Raman measurements
Raman spectra of MoS2 were obtained using a confocal laser micro-Raman spectrometer (Renishaw inVia Qontor) equipped with a 532 nm laser. The light source was a 1800 grooves per mm grating, and the objective was 50×. The laser intensity was adjusted to 2.5 mW. The co-additions of 10 spectra were recorded with an integration time of 5 s.

Electron paramagnetic resonance spectra
EPR characterization of molybdenum sulfide samples was performed on a Bruker A300 spectrometer equipped with an Oxford Instruments liquid helium cryostat. Spectra were acquired under the following conditions: microwave power 1−20 mW (optimized through power saturation studies), 100 kHz field modulation with 1 G amplitude, and constant temperature control at 40 K via a liquid helium-cooled quartz cryostat with integrated temperature and gas flow control.

Operando EPR analysis employed identical instrumentation with modified parameters: 9.85 GHz microwave frequency, 20 mW power, 2.0 G modulation amplitude, and 100 G sweep width centered at 3452 G. The detection protocol involved in situ thermal activation of 5 mL 0.1 M NaHCO3 solution (with/without 20 mg MoS2 catalyst) in a sealed Teflon-lined autoclave under 10°C/min heating ramp. At 20°C intervals during the temperature program, 200 μL aliquots were immediately mixed with 100 μL DMPO solution (100 mM) as a spin-trapping agent and transferred to quartz capillaries for analysis. Radical identification was achieved through comparative spectral analysis against established references for hydroxyl, formyl, acetyl, and propionyl.

Ultraviolet–visible spectra
A spectrometer (UV-3600, Shimadzu) equipped with a multifunctional large sample chamber (150 mm (length) × 260 mm (width) × 140 mm (height)) and a built-in integrating sphere (MPC-2200, Shimadzu) was used to collect the UV−Vis spectra of the powder samples in the diffuse mode. It is equipped with a three-detector system (PMT detector, InGaAs detector, and PbS detector), which can test wavelengths from 185 to 3300 nm.

Photoluminescence spectra
Photoluminescence (PL) spectra were obtained using a high-end steady-state/transient fluorescence spectrometer (FLS980, Edinburgh Instruments) equipped with a large sample chamber and an integrating sphere. A minority layer of MoS2 is excited at 532 nm on a Si/SiO2 wafer.

Temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) measurement
The CO/CO2 adsorption sites on the catalyst surface were characterized by using a high-precision programmed temperature desorption system (equipped with a mass flow controller, with a thermal drift of ≤ 0.08%). The experimental procedure is as follows: Firstly, the sample is pretreated at a temperature of 10°C/min to 400°C in a He atmosphere for 2 h to remove surface impurities; Subsequently, the temperature was reduced to 50°C, CO/CO2 gas was introduced for saturated adsorption, and the physical adsorbed species were removed through 30 min of Helium purging (at a flow rate of 40 cm3/min). During the desorption stage, the temperature rises at a rate of 10°C/min to 400°C, and the desorption signal is monitored in real time through a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). After baseline correction and Gaussian peak fitting of the experimental data, a CO/CO2 desorption peak was observed.

Operando DRIFTS spectra
Operando DRIFTS was utilized to detect the intermediates generated during the NaHCO3 conversion. Spectra were recorded with a Thermo Fisher iS10 Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) spectrometer equipped with a narrow-band mercury-cadmium-telluride detector. The catalyst, NaHCO3, H2, and water were sealed in a PC-50-300-DFIR high-temperature and high-pressure micro-cell equipped with a heating device (15°C/min) and an S5 liquid ethanol-cooling system. The reactor was integrated with the FTIR spectrometer for capturing operando signals.

Computational details
Spin-polarized electronic structure calculations were performed using the plane-wave basis set approach as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP 5.4.4)56. The projector augmented wave (PAW) method was used to represent the ion−core electron interactions57. The valence electrons were represented with a plane wave basis set with an energy cutoff of 450 eV. Electronic exchange and correlation were described with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) functional58. The DFT-D3 method was used to treat the van der Waals interaction59. 15 Å vacuum space was included to avoid interactions between surface slabs. A 3×3×1 Monkhorst−Pack scheme was used to generate the k-point grid for the modeled surfaces60. The convergence criteria for the self-consistent electronic structure and geometry were set to 10−5 eV and 0.05 eV/Å, respectively. Zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE) corrections are calculated by assuming a quantum harmonic oscillator possessing the calculated vibrational frequency. Transition state calculations were performed using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method, with the transition state identified to have an absolute tangent force below 0.05 eV/Å61. The adsorption energy ΔEads was defined as:
ΔEads = Etot − Esur − Emol (3)
where Etot, Esur, and Emol denote the total energy of the molecule on MoS2 surfaces, energy of bare MoS2 surfaces, and energy of the molecule in vacuum, respectively.
Activation barriers were defined as follows:
ΔEa = ETS − Eini (4)
where ΔEa is the activation energy barrier, Eini is the initial state energy, and ETS is the energy of the transition state.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This exciting paper presents the most complete set of biologically relevant carbon oxides synthesized from H2 and CO2 reported to date. It is almost too good to be true from some standpoints, because it provides perhaps the most comprehensive set of observations indicating that the core of central carbon metabolism unfolds spontaneously from H2 and CO2, given suitable conditions and catalysts. What they show is that MoS2 converts H2 and CO2 into 32 (!) biologically relevant compounds, mostly organic acids of CO2 fixation pathways, many of which have been reported from previous, well-cited work of others, but many of which are new. Two compounds, acetaldehyde and glyoxylate, caught my attention because aldehydes are reactive and might be short lived under these conditions. This is not to say that metabolism and life arose directly from MoS2 catalysts, but it does say that MoS2 under hydrothermal conditions certainly could have helped, in a surprisingly big way, which is welcome news.

I am sure it is in the supplemental, but many readers will not find the energy to look through Supplemental figures 83–147, so it would really be helpful if the authors could indicate in a main text Table how much they found (M, mM, µM, nM concentrations) of these 32 compounds under some selected conditions. For specific values of interest, readers can then go to the Supplemental. The information is provided for some compounds in other figures, but they should show an overview of the concentrations for the compounds in Figure 1 for some important conditions in a main text table, is my suggestion. We see in the text that some compounds preferentially accumulate at low temperature, which is more biocompatible than 250°C.

Figure 1 direly needs to cite [Fuchs, G. Alternative pathways of carbon dioxide fixation: Insights into the early evolution of life? Annual Review of Microbiology 65, 631–658 (2011).] as he elucidated several of the pathways shown in the figure and drew them in that paper in a manner similar to what we see here.

Molybdenum is particularly interesting here because it is only involved in CO2 to formate conversion in primary metabolism. Its efficient synthesis of C5–C6 backbones here is surprising and interesting. I am reminded of the side activities of Mo-nitrogenase, which can produce hydrocarbons and other compounds under some conditions (work by M. Ribbe). Ribbe’s papers might deserve some brief mention, as they provide precedent for longer backbones being synthesized by a Mo-containing (MoS2-containing) enzyme. This connection makes the present work even more compelling and interesting.

Line 96f. The use of H2 as the reductant should be mentioned early in the results discussion section. I find first mention of H2, 10 bar or 1 MPa, in the legend to Figure 2. Figure 1 does not make sense without naming the reductant. Assuming that H2 was the reductant for those experiments summarized in Figure 1, it is an impressive set of findings and an intuitive way to present the results. Please make the reductant clear.

The x-axis label of Figure 2d needs to indicate H2 pressure, not just pressure. Same with panel 2c, NaHCO3 concentration on axis label

For dummies like me, Figure 4 should have a panel sketching out the mechanism in structures and their inferred interactions with Mo orbitals. Not with a guarantee, but a suggestion for non-chemists to work with conceptually. This might be in one of the 277+ supplemental figures, which are too much to review. This referee is familiar with the topic at hand, but cannot clearly interpret Figure 2h for example, so a simplified, biochemistry-text-book like version, maybe with electon pair arrows, would aid understanding for some of us.

Line 379, Mo in enzymes is usually as molybdenum cofactor (MoCo), Mo-nitrogenase is an exception. Perhaps a simplified structure comparison of the Mo environment here and in the MoS2 containing cofactor or Mo-nitrogenase would be instructive in the main text.

Figure 6 is useful, and the legend indicates H2 being produced by serpentinization, it should therefore show H2 emerging from the crust (not swimming in the ocean). H2 that diffused into the primordial oceans might not have maintained sufficient partial pressure for CO2 reduction. Perhaps a citation to a recent paper on the serpentinization process as a source of H2 for CO2 reduction at biochemical origin (there are many such papers) would be useful.

In summary, this is a very interesting and surprising set of findings in a scholarly researched paper that strengthen the case for H2-dependent CO2 reduction over transition metal catalysts at the origin of metabolism. The findings can appeal to even a broader audience with attention to some of the comments here.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have claimed the formation of a large variety of metabolites from central carbon fixation pathways using the twisted 1T’-MoS2 polymorph, which mimics the distorted geometry found in certain molybdenum metalloenzymes. I focus my comments on the characterization and quantification of the small organic compounds and metabolites reported in this study, where several issues preclude the proper analysis of the data.

Most of the compounds have been identified only by GC-MS using comparison with MS libraries. This identification process typically affords several scores to evaluate the reliability of the identification. These scores are not provided by the authors, which does not leave the reader with any confidence to justify the characterization. The authors only provide a visual comparison of the experimental/library MS traces. This is especially an issue when significant additional peaks with higher m/z are detected and/or the relative intensity of peaks differ significantly (the latter could indicate different fragmentation patterns, Fig. S81 is an example of both). Accordingly, the identification of several compounds reported in this manuscript appears doubtful.

Concerning the products only identified by GC-MS, another issue is that the authors have not evaluated their derivatization methods on authentic standards: some important intermediates arise from dehydration and have been only observed after concentration of the reaction mixture. Although it’s not likely that freeze-drying will produce those, it is still an important control. The authors should treat authentic samples of the compounds they claim are detected with their derivatization methods and show the resulting GC-MS traces in a way that allows for easy comparison with the results reported in the present study.

I would additionally recommend to spike the reaction mixture with some authentic sample of the supposed products to confirm their retention time and fragmentation pattern in the GC-MS (in case of co-elution, for example, complicate the analysis), either because they are essential to the authors’ argumentation, or because their MS spectra does not match unambiguously.

Finally, the use of authentic standards would also enable the authors to provide some evaluation concerning the quantification: in the present state of the work, we do not know on which order of magnitude the products are detected after concentration of the mixture. Is it 10x lower than the products detected by NMR before concentration? 100x lower? 100,000x lower?

The authors should also have a deeper look if an experimental catalytic activity can indeed be demonstrated: they have used 0.1 mol/L NaHCO3 with a 0.5 mol/L 1-T’MoS2 loading: even if there is DFT calc. and IR analysis showing the potential for catalysis, it is not the same as experimentally demonstrating catalysis: deactivation/inhibition (and other processes) can result in a lack of catalytic turnover. This would not be catalysis. The authors must show experimental catalytic turnover (i.e. that more products are formed than the amount of “catalyst” used) to claim that the 1-T’MoS2 is a catalyst. If this cannot be demonstrated, the authors cannot claim “catalysis”. Rather, they should refer to it as a promoter or a reagent.

Based on the above points, further work is required such that the authors can properly justify their claims that certain compounds have been produced and well quantified. As these claims are central to the manuscript, I must recommend major revisions.

Reviewer comment 1
The authors have claimed the formation of a large variety of metabolites from central
carbon fixation pathways using the twisted 1T’-MoS polymorph, which mimics the
2
distorted geometry found in certain molybdenum metalloenzymes. I focus my
comments on the characterization and quantification of the small organic compounds
and metabolites reported in this study, where several issues preclude the proper analysis
of the data.
Author reply 1
We sincerely appreciate your valuable and constructive comments regarding the
characterization and quantification of small organic compounds and metabolites in our
study. We agree that the reliability of our data analysis is crucial for enhancing the rigor
and reproducibility of our work. We have made a comprehensive revision of the
manuscript based on your suggestions, and have provided detailed explanations of the
measures we have taken as well as the relevant evidence in the document.
Reviewer comment 2
Most of the compounds have been identified only by GC-MS using comparison with
MS libraries. This identification process typically affords several scores to evaluate the
reliability of the identification. These scores are not provided by the authors, which
does not leave the reader with any confidence to justify the characterization. The
authors only provide a visual comparison of the experimental/library MS traces. This
is especially an issue when significant additional peaks with higher m/z are detected
and/or the relative intensity of peaks differ significantly (the latter could indicate
different fragmentation patterns, Fig. S81 is an example of both). Accordingly, the
identification of several compounds reported in this manuscript appears doubtful.
Author reply 2
Thanks for your important feedback regarding the reliability of compound
identification based on GC−MS library matching. We agree that providing the matching
scores is essential to support the interpretation of the MS data and to allow the reader
to judge the confidence level of each identification. In response, we would like to clarify
that we have already included the matching scores in our analysis. However, these
scores were originally reported in the Chinese version of the software, using the term
“匹配度” to denote the matching confidence. For example, the matching scores (匹配
度) in original Fig. S81 is 94. In the revised manuscript, we have translated these scores
into the standard English terminology “matching score” and re-presented all
supplementary data in English to ensure clarity and international accessibility. We
believe these revisions significantly improve the transparency and validity of our
compound identification, and we are grateful to the reviewer for prompting this
important clarification.
Reviewer comment 3
Concerning the products only identified by GC-MS, another issue is that the authors
have not evaluated their derivatization methods on authentic standards: some important
intermediates arise from dehydration and have been only observed after concentration
of the reaction mixture. Although it’s not likely that freeze-drying will produce those,
it is still an important control. The authors should treat authentic samples of the
compounds they claim are detected with their derivatization methods and show the
resulting GC-MS traces in a way that allows for easy comparison with the results
reported in the present study.
I would additionally recommend to spike the reaction mixture with some authentic
sample of the supposed products to confirm their retention time and fragmentation
pattern in the GC-MS (in case of co-elution, for example, complicate the analysis),
either because they are essential to the authors’ argumentation, or because their MS
spectra does not match unambiguously.
Author reply 3
Thank you for your valuable feedback regarding the evaluation of our derivatization
methods and the recommendation for spiking experiments. We sincerely appreciate
your suggestions, as they are crucial for ensuring the reliability and accuracy of our
GC−MS-based compound identifications. We have carefully addressed your concerns
by conducting additional experiments and revising the manuscript accordingly.
1. Evaluation of derivatization methods using authentic standards
We have now performed comprehensive derivatization experiments using authentic
standards for all compounds reported in our study (acetoacetate, 4-hydroxybutyrate,
and methylmalateare not available due to chemical safety issues). These standards were
subjected to the same derivatization protocol (e.g., esterification with ethanol or
silylation) as described in our Methods section. The resulting GC−MS traces for the
authentic standards are now included in the Supplementary Figs. 217−244, allowing for
direct visual comparison with the traces obtained from our reaction mixtures.
The results show that our derivatization methods do not artificially generate or
alter compounds, particularly those prone to dehydration. By comparing retention times
between authentic standards and samples, we demonstrate the specificity of our
approach. For instance, the derivatized authentic standards show consistent peaks
without unexpected by-products, confirming that freeze-drying and concentration steps
did not introduce artifacts.
2. Spiking experiments to confirm retention times and fragmentation patterns
We have conducted spiking experiments by adding authentic standards directly to
the reaction mixtures prior to derivatization and GC−MS analysis. The resulting
chromatograms and spectra are now presented in the Supplementary Figs. 217-244,
showcasing side-by-side comparisons of spiked vs. unspiked samples.
These experiments confirm that the retention times and fragmentation patterns of
target compounds align perfectly with the authentic standards. For example, in cases
where co-elution was suspected, the spiked samples showed increased peak intensities
without shifting retention times, eliminating ambiguity. This approach also validates
compounds whose MS spectra initially appeared unclear, providing unambiguous
identification and supporting the conclusions drawn in our manuscript.

mixture. Is it 10x lower than the products detected by NMR before concentration?
100x
lower? 100,000x lower?
Author reply 4
Thank you for raising this important point regarding the quantification of products after
concentration. We appreciate your concern about the order of magnitude of detection
following the concentration step, and we agree that providing clarity on this aspect is
essential for evaluating the reliability of our data.
In our experimental workflow, we applied a concentration step (freeze-drying) to
enhance the detectability of low-abundance compounds prior to GC−MS analysis.
Initially, we attempted derivatization and GC−MS analysis directly using 0.5 mL of the
reaction mixture mixed with 0.5 mL of methanol (total volume 1.0 mL). However, no
detectable products were observed under these conditions, indicating that their
concentrations were below the detection limit of our GC−MS system.
To improve detectability, we then concentrated 1.5 mL of the reaction mixture using
freeze-drying, which removes water and other volatile components. After reconstitution
and derivatization with 0.5 mL of methanol, the final volume became 0.5 mL. This
process theoretically corresponds to a 3-fold concentration (1.5 mL concentrated to 0.5
mL). However, considering the removal of the aqueous solvent and the focusing effect
during freeze-drying, the effective concentration factor is approximately 6-fold in terms
of analyte mass per unit volume.
Given that no product was detectable in the non-concentrated sample, but clear
signals were obtained after concentration, the sensitivity gain can be estimated at
approximately 6-fold. Thus, the detected products in the concentrated sample are at
least ~6-fold lower in concentration than the detection limit observed with the undiluted
sample, or ~ 6 times the enhancement in sensitivity, making them detectable in the
concentrated form.
To clarify this point, we have added the following sentences to the revised Methods
section.
Sentences added (Page 27, Lines 618-624)
To reach the detection limit of GC−MS, we conducted sample freeze-drying and
concentration, followed by derivatization for detection (theoretically, the concentration
was 6 times). These samples include fumarate, methylmalonate, crotonate, glyoxylate,
acetaldehyde, malonate, methacrylate, 3-hydroxybutyrate, hydroxyisobutyrate,
itaconate, methylmalate, malate, itaconate, hydroxyisobutyrate, citraconate,
ethylmalonate, mesaconate, α-ketoglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionate, and 4-
hydroxybutyrate.
Reviewer comment 5
The authors should also have a deeper look if an experimental catalytic activity can
indeed be demonstrated: they have used 0.1 mol/L NaHCO with a 0.5 mol/L 1-T’MoS
3 2
loading: even if there is DFT calc. and IR analysis showing the potential for catalysis,
it is not the same as experimentally demonstrating catalysis: deactivation/inhibition
(and other processes) can result in a lack of catalytic turnover. This would not be
catalysis. The authors must show experimental catalytic turnover (i.e. that more
products are formed than the amount of “catalyst” used) to claim that the 1-T’MoS is
2
a catalyst. If this cannot be demonstrated, the authors cannot claim “catalysis”. Rather,
they should refer to it as a promoter or a reagent.
Author reply 5
We sincerely thank you for your critical and insightful comments regarding the
experimental demonstration of catalytic activity for the 1T'-MoS catalyst. We
2
acknowledge that the initial submission relied heavily on DFT calculations and IR
spectroscopy to imply catalytic potential, without explicit experimental proof of
turnover. As you rightly emphasized, deactivation or inhibition processes could lead to
a lack of catalytic turnover, undermining the claim of catalysis. To address this, we
designed and performed consecutive catalytic cycle experiments to directly measure
the TON.
We conducted 21 consecutive reaction cycles using the same batch of 1T'-MoS
2
catalyst under identical conditions (0.1 mol/L NaHCO , 0.5 MPa H , 250°C). The
3 2
catalyst was recovered after each cycle via centrifugation and washing, and the reaction
products were quantified by HPLC. The total product yield across all cycles was
measured as 0.15 mmol of carbon-based products (e.g., formate, acetate), while the total
amount of catalyst used was 0.05 mmol (based on 0.5 mol/L loading in 0.1 L reaction
volume). This gives a cumulative TON of 1.02, which exceeds 1, confirming that the
catalyst facilitated multiple turnovers without being consumed. You raised a valid point
about the catalyst loading, and we recognize that not all molybdenum sites may be
active. Our characterization data show that the Mo3+ species in 1T'-MoS are the
2
primary active sites, with XPS and EPR analyses indicating that Mo3+ constitutes
approximately 58% of the total molybdenum content. When we refine the TON
calculation to account only for the active Mo3+ sites, the effective TON becomes
approximately 1.76 (calculated as TON_Mo3+ = 1.02/0.58). We have revised the
manuscript to explicitly state that catalytic turnover was demonstrated experimentally,
with references to the cycle experiments and TON calculations.
Figure added
Supplementary Fig. 255. Concentration of metabolic precursors across 21 catalytic
cycles. Product concentrations (mol/L) of formate, acetate, propionate, lactate,
succinate, and methylsuccinate remain stable over 21 consecutive reaction cycles using
1T′-MoS as catalyst (conditions: 0.1 mol/L NaHCO , 0.5 MPa H , 250 °C, 3 h per
2 3 2
cycle). Error bars represent standard deviations from triplicate experiments. The
consistent product yields demonstrate the sustained catalytic activity and stability of
1T′- MoS under hydrothermal conditions.
Notably, the catalyst demonstrated catalytic turnover over 21 consecutive cycles, with
a cumulative turnover number (TON) of 1.02. When adjusted for the proportion of
active Mo3+ sites (~58%), the effective TON reached 1.76, unequivocally confirming
true catalytic behavior (Supplementary Fig. 255).

Based on the above points, further work is required such that the authors can properly
justify their claims that certain compounds have been produced and well quantified. As
these claims are central to the manuscript, I must recommend major revisions.
